{"result":"# The Rust Programming Language and Memory Safety

Rust is a general-purpose language that balances performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety [1]. Graydon Hoare began it as a personal project in 2006, and Mozilla Research sponsored it from 2009 [2]. It was first publicly released in 2010, and version 1.0 arrived in 2015 [2].

Memory safety protects programs from software bugs and security vulnerabilities, such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. Java enforces this through runtime checks of array bounds and pointer dereferences [3]. By contrast, C, C++, and Fortran allow unchecked pointer arithmetic, which makes them memory-unsafe [3].

Rust's syntax resembles C++, yet it guarantees memory safety without a garbage collector [2]. Rather than classes or inheritance, it relies on structs, enums, traits, and methods [1]. This blend of C++-like control and enforced safety is central to its design.
